Ulysses S. Grant. The commanding general of the Union Army during the American Civil War's final campaigns and the eighteenth president of the United States from eighteen sixty-nine to eighteen seventy-seven. A career soldier of modest ambition who achieved his greatest fame in warfare, Grant earned a reputation as a relentless tactician willing to absorb casualties to win, summed up in his philosophy of attrition. His presidency, though marred by corruption scandals, oversaw the final phase of Reconstruction and aimed to protect the civil rights of freed slaves, though with declining congressional support.

Grant rose from obscurity to become commanding general of all Union armies in March eighteen sixty-four, after years of lesser officers had failed to decisively defeat Robert E. Lee. He orchestrated the strategy of simultaneous pressure on multiple fronts. While William Tecumseh Sherman marched toward Atlanta, Grant pressed Lee in Virginia, denying the Confederacy the ability to shift forces. Grant won the war of attrition at Petersburg from eighteen sixty-four to eighteen sixty-five, surrounding Lee's army and forcing its surrender at Appomattox in April eighteen sixty-five, effectively ending the Civil War.

Elected president in eighteen sixty-eight as a Republican, Grant championed the Reconstruction Acts, the Fifteenth Amendment guaranteeing voting rights regardless of race, and federal intervention to suppress the Ku Klux Klan. His presidency suffered from scandals including the Whiskey Ring and corruption among his cabinet members and associates, though he himself was never personally implicated in fraud. He left office in eighteen seventy-seven with his popularity diminished. He spent his final years writing his memoirs, published posthumously, which remain among the finest military autobiographies in American literature.
